analysis.one_liner: Creates fines and the right to sue airlines for harming or stranding passengers with disabilities.
analysis.headline: The bill to let disabled air passengers sue airlines and require fines for damaged wheelchairs and denied boarding has sat in the House Transportation Committee since June 2026 with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Air Carrier Access Act of 1986 bans disability discrimination by airlines, but passengers cannot sue and enforcement has been complaint-by-complaint. This bill would require the government to fine airlines for specific harms — destroyed or delayed wheelchairs, physical harm, failure to provide boarding help, denied boarding, mishandled service animals — and would create a private right of action letting passengers sue in federal court for compensatory and punitive damages, with attorney's fees for the prevailing party and no requirement to file a complaint with the government first. It would also let the Justice Department sue airlines that show a pattern of discrimination.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers with disabilities — including veterans, wheelchair and scooter users, and service animal handlers — who today can file a complaint with the Department of Transportation but cannot take an airline to court when a wheelchair is destroyed or boarding assistance fails. The bill gives them fines on the airline's side of the ledger and a courtroom remedy on theirs, with the airline on the hook for attorney's fees if they win.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Transportation to assess a civil penalty for, at minimum, each incident of delayed, lost, or significantly damaged wheelchairs or scooters, physical harm to or fatal injury of a passenger, failure to provide required aisle-chair boarding assistance, noncompliant denial of boarding or service animal access, and gross negligence toward a passenger with disabilities [S2].

Creates a private right of action: any aggrieved person may sue an air carrier in federal district court within two years for appropriate relief including compensatory and punitive damages, with no requirement to exhaust administrative remedies first [S2].
Requires courts to award reasonable attorney's fees, expert fees, and court costs to the prevailing party, and bars the new remedy from limiting stronger state or federal disability protections [S2].

Requires referral to the Attorney General when there is reasonable cause to believe an airline engages in a pattern or practice of discrimination, and empowers the Attorney General to sue airlines on behalf of aggrieved individuals for equitable relief, damages, and civil penalties [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, domestic and foreign, which would face per-incident civil penalties and courtroom liability, including punitive damages and plaintiffs' attorney's fees. Those costs could show up modestly in fares, and carriers would bear new litigation exposure on routes they operate today without it.

drawbacks.text: Litigation exposure is broad: the private right of action covers violations of any DOT or FAA regulation under the ACAA, carries punitive damages and fee-shifting, and does not require passengers to try the administrative complaint process first, which carriers and some scholars argue invites costly suits over minor violations and pressures airlines to settle [S2].

Airline groups have historically opposed ACAA private rights of action on the ground that DOT complaint enforcement is free to passengers and already produces penalties, and that the real cost of litigation will be passed through to all travelers — the record provided here contains no hearing or debate in which these objections were weighed [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The remedy addresses a real gap: unlike the Americans with Disabilities Act, the ACAA has no private right of action, so passengers with disabilities have had no practical court remedy when wheelchairs are destroyed or boarding assistance fails, and DOT enforcement has been slow complaint-by-complaint. The cost side is real but conventional — fee-shifting and punitive damages are standard tools in other civil rights statutes, and the burden falls on airlines that caused the harm. The main design risk is breadth: covering every regulatory violation without an exhaustion requirement could produce litigation over minor infractions, and the bill never got a hearing where that could be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which has taken no action on it since; it is waiting for a hearing or markup that has not been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Dina Titus introduced the bill on June 18, 2026, joined by Reps. Cohen, Brownley, Norton, and Carson, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1] [S2].
The bill's only recorded actions since June 18, 2026 are its introduction and committee referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history [S4].
The bill has 6 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines benefit from the bill's inaction so far: no hearing or vote means no fines, no private lawsuits, and no added litigation exposure while the current complaint-based system continues.

for.name: Rep. Dina Titus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Air Carrier Access Amendments Act of 2026 and referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

for.name: Reps. Steve Cohen, Julia Brownley, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and André Carson
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: Additional House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after introduction, bringing the total to 6.

against.name: Rep. Sam Graves
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its June 2026 referral; the bill has not left the committee.

against.name: Airlines and airline trade associations
against.what_they_did: Benefit from the bill's stalling; carriers have historically opposed adding a private right of action under the Air Carrier Access Act, and no hearing has been held where the bill's remedies would be advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a House Democrat (6 of 217); no House Republican has cosponsored, and no roll-call votes have occurred, so the partisan shape is so far one-sided rather than tested.

industries.industry: Airlines (passenger air carriers, domestic and foreign)
industries.note: The bill would impose per-incident civil penalties for damaged wheelchairs, passenger injuries, failed boarding assistance, and denied boarding, and would expose carriers to compensatory and punitive damages suits with fee-shifting. The industry's interest runs against disabled passengers, who currently have no court remedy; its savings from that gap are the bill's target.

industries.industry: Disability travel and mobility-device users (veterans and service animal handlers)
industries.note: Not an industry but the affected constituency: passengers who today rely on slow DOT complaints would gain enforceable court remedies and attorney's fees. Their interest runs alongside the bill's.

industries.industry: Disability rights organizations and legal-aid plaintiffs' bar
industries.note: A private right of action with fee-shifting would fund representation for disabled passengers and strengthen disability-rights enforcement; these groups have backed similar ACAA amendments in past Congresses.

analysis.trajectory: With only 6 Democratic cosponsors and no action from the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee more than four months after referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote in this Congress; most disability-protection bills at this stage die quietly when the session ends on January 3, 2027, unless a larger transportation package picks up its provisions.
